concept.name: Confirmation
concept.definition: A confirmation is the inclusion of a transaction in a mined/validated block; each additional block built on top counts as another confirmation and exponentially reduces the probability that the transaction is reversed.
concept.intuition: Each confirmation is another layer of concrete poured over your transaction — one layer can be broken through, six is conventional vault-grade.
concept.mechanics: In proof-of-work chains, the probability that an attacker catches up to the honest chain decays exponentially with the number of confirmations (Nakamoto's analysis), so receivers wait for N blocks (conventionally 6 for Bitcoin, ≈60 minutes) before treating payment as safe. On proof-of-stake Ethereum, confirmations culminate in explicit finality after two epochs.
concept.failure_modes: Accepting zero-confirmation transactions exposes the receiver to double-spends; during chain reorganizations, even confirmed transactions can temporarily be dropped back to pending.
concept.misconceptions: 'Confirmed' does not mean 'irreversible' on PoW chains — it is a confidence gradient, which is why high-value transfers wait for more confirmations. The 6-block rule is a convention, not a protocol guarantee.
concept.example: A merchant accepting a $50,000 BTC payment waits for 6 confirmations (~1 hour) because reversing 6 blocks would require an attacker to privately out-mine the honest network for an hour, an astronomically unlikely feat at honest-majority hash rate.

citations.source: Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System (whitepaper)
